headings.title: Overview of Patient Assisted Devices
headings.content: Patient assisted devices encompass a wide range of technological and mechanical tools designed to maintain or improve an individual's functioning and independence. In modern healthcare, these tools bridge the gap between complete physical dependence and self-care. They span from simple mobility aids like canes to complex motorized systems and health informatics integrations. Understanding these devices helps nurses reduce the physical strain of manual handling and promotes safer rehabilitation outcomes for patients across Nigerian healthcare facilities.

headings.title: Mobility and Transfer Equipment
headings.content:
Mobility aids are fundamental in preventing caregiver injuries and ensuring safe patient movement. Common equipment includes transfer boards, mechanical lifts, sliding sheets, and gait belts. When selecting a transfer device, the nurse must evaluate the patient's weight-bearing capacity, cognitive status, and upper body strength. 

- **Gait belts**: Used for supporting patients during ambulation or standing transfers.
- **Slide sheets**: Reduce friction when repositioning patients in bed.
- **Mechanical lifts**: Hydraulic or battery-operated hoists for totally dependent patients.
- **Transfer boards**: Bridge the gap between a bed and a wheelchair for seated transfers.

headings.title: Automated Wheelchairs and Smart Mobility
headings.content: Modern wheelchairs have evolved far beyond standard manual frames. Automated and smart wheelchairs incorporate microprocessors, sensors, and power-assist mechanisms to accommodate patients with severe neuromuscular impairments. These chairs can navigate tight spaces, detect obstacles, and adjust seating angles to prevent pressure ulcers. Nurses must ensure that patients using smart wheelchairs understand basic troubleshooting, battery maintenance, and braking systems to avoid accidental collisions or sudden power loss.

headings.title: Robotics in Rehabilitation and Patient Care
headings.content: Robotic technology plays an increasingly vital role in physical therapy and long-term care units. Exoskeletons and robotic limbs help stroke survivors and spinal cord injury patients relearn proper walking patterns through repetitive, computer-guided movements. These systems reduce the physical burden on physical therapists while providing precise feedback on joint angles and muscle engagement. Nurses collaborate with rehabilitation teams to monitor skin integrity at contact points where robotic braces strap onto the patient's limbs.

headings.title: Integration with Health Information Systems and EHRs
headings.content: Many modern assistive devices now connect directly to hospital electronic health record systems through wireless networks. Smart beds, automated infusion pumps, and digital mobility monitors transmit real-time data on patient status, vitals, and device usage directly to the nursing station. This connectivity allows for automated charting, reduces manual documentation errors, and triggers immediate alerts if a patient attempts to leave a bed unsafely. Nurses must verify that data feeds are functioning correctly and maintain data privacy standards.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Patient Safety Considerations
headings.content: Introducing any assistive device requires a thorough nursing assessment of the patient's physical, cognitive, and emotional readiness. A device that works well for one patient may cause confusion or frustration for another, particularly among older adults with cognitive impairment. Safety checks must be performed routinely, including inspecting cords, checking brakes, and ensuring proper fit. Furthermore, nurses must educate both the patient and their family members on correct operation to prevent accidental injuries.
